 TELECOMMUNICATIONS Services of Trinidad and Tobago (TSTT) has threatened legal action to recover nearly $12 million from NOBIS Group Ltd for alleged breaches of contract, claiming it paid in full for a digital identity-verification platform that never became operational.
 In a pre-action letter dated November 18, 2026, attorneys Suraj Sakal and Angel Jaggernath demanded the return of TT$5.95 million and US$875,000, alleging that the system accepted false identification documents and could not reliably verify customers’ identities.
 “The Platform has never been brought into live operation, it cannot reliably perform its core function of verifying the identity of a customer, and more than seven months after the contractual deadline it remains unfit for production use,” the letter stated.
 Addressed to NOBIS chief executive Ryan Kevin Chin Sang and its board, the letter formally declares a material breach and demands repayment within 14 days of receipt.
 The agreement, executed on February 5, required NOBIS to implement, configure and bring the electronic Know Your Customer (e-KYC) platform into operation by April 1.
 The system was intended to capture government-issued identification, extract and validate personal information, perform facial recognition and liveness checks, and connect with TSTT’s customer registration and other systems.
 TSTT’s attorneys said the contract expressly entitled the company to a refund if NOBIS missed the implementation deadline. Any extension required a delay attributable to TSTT and mutual written agreement. They maintained neither condition existed.
 According to the letter, TSTT paid the entire fee in February, before receiving access to a test environment or conducting acceptance testing. Access requested from February 9 was allegedly provided only on March 9. TSTT said it never received access to a production environment.
 Testing allegedly exposed fundamental failures: the platform accepted false, expired and non-government identification documents and allowed someone to pass verification using another person’s identification with the user’s own photograph.
 “For a platform whose purpose is to verify identity, those defects go to the root of what our client contracted for,” the attorneys wrote.
 Other alleged failures included ineffective facial verification, liveness detection and identity matching, unreliable e-mail verification and difficulties completing registration across devices.
 TSTT also alleged security weaknesses. The platform’s application programming interface reportedly returned hashed passwords and secrets, while credential regeneration failed: replacement credentials did not work and the old secret remained valid.
 The attorneys said NOBIS failed to provide promised vulnerability and penetration-testing reports, written authorisation for TSTT’s security scan, or independent assurance that its security practices met recognised standards.
 TSTT warned NOBIS on March 24 that implementation appeared at risk and requested remediation plans and security-testing evidence.
 According to the letter, NOBIS responded on March 25 that the platform had been fully deployed, configured and made available by March 10 in a functional, operational condition capable of immediate use.
 NOBIS maintained it had satisfied the implementation requirement and disputed any entitlement to a refund.
 TSTT rejected that position, arguing that availability in a testing environment did not constitute going live. It also rejected NOBIS’s contention that outstanding integration matters were TSTT’s responsibility, saying integration support formed part of NOBIS’s contractual obligations.
 More than 30 defects, gaps and requests were subsequently logged. Although some were addressed, TSTT alleged the core verification and security problems remained unresolved. An October 5 readiness assessment found the platform unsuitable for production, the letter stated.
 NOBIS also allegedly failed to answer correspondence, attend weekly progress meetings and engage despite repeated requests.
 The letter raised further questions about representations preceding the contract.
 TSTT alleged that assurances that the platform was fully tested and ready for deployment were false. It also claimed NOBIS demonstrated third-party, uncustomised open-source software that differed from what was subsequently supplied.
 The attorneys said NOBIS had never produced documentation establishing ownership of, or authority to license, the underlying technology.
 They also sought an explanation for banking details naming Nimble Mobile Limited in connection with an initial, returned transfer, noting apparent ownership and management links between the companies.
 TSTT is additionally investigating whether NOBIS or its representatives acted with anyone then employed by TSTT to cause it loss through unlawful means. The letter reserves possible claims against others, depending on that investigation.
 NOBIS has seven days to indicate whether it will refund the fee or agree to mediation, and 28 days to provide a full response.
 If it fails to refund the money or refer the dispute to mediation within that period, TSTT says it will commence High Court proceedings without further notice, seeking repayment or alternative remedies, including damages, interest and costs.
 “Litigation should be a last resort. Our client would prefer to resolve this matter without recourse to the Court,” the attorneys stated.
 E-mails to Chin Sang were not immediately answered yesterday.
